title: Transfer a datum height to a far post with a water level, holding the jar's water at the line while marking
instruction: Use the water level to mark the height of the datum post's black line on the far post with the red marker, then put the jar and the hose end back in their stands.
context: Carpenters (about 889,700 US jobs in 2025, BLS; O*NET 47-2031.00 lists "Verify trueness of structure, using plumb bob and level" among their tasks) carry a height around a room or a site to set a ledger, a deck or a run of cabinets on one datum when the floor is not level and the far point is out of a spirit level's reach. A water level does this without a line of sight (Fine Homebuilding, "Making and Using Water Levels", 1994). The water in the jar and in the clear end tube stands at one height, and the jar is far wider, so the water follows the jar: its water is held on the datum line by hand while the far end's water surface is marked. The end must go up before the jar and come down after it, or water runs out of the end's mouth. Here the far post stands on a 2.5 cm pad, so copying the line's height above the floor would put the mark 2.5 cm off.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y to the robot's left), heights above the table. Datum post (fixed): pine, 4 by 4 cm, 18 cm tall, centered at (30, 23.5), a black datum line 2 mm wide painted all round at 13.0 cm. Far post (fixed): pine, 4 by 4 cm, centered at (30, -23.5), standing on a gray pad 12 by 12 by 2.5 cm, top at 18 cm; a plywood shelf on its inboard face, floor at 4 cm with a 1 cm rim on three sides, 5.2 by 5.6 cm inside; a red sliding marker on its front face, held by friction, with a grip tab 4.5 by 2.4 by 2 cm sticking out toward the robot from its outboard half (8 mm off center) and a thin pointer reaching in front of a tube standing on the shelf; the pointer's top edge is the mark, at 9.2 cm at the start. Water level: a clear round plastic jar 10 cm across and 10 cm tall (9.4 cm inside) with a vented lid and a black carry handle across it (a bar 5 by 2.5 cm, 3 cm tall), 150 g, standing in a plywood tray (its stand: 1 cm rim, 12 cm square inside) centered at (22, 14); 1.2 m of 9.5 mm (0.375 inch) bore clear vinyl hose from a fitting in the jar's bottom, coiled on the table at (22, 0); the hose end: a clear acrylic tube (12.7 mm bore, 9 cm long, from 3 to 12 cm above the stick's bottom) taped to the front face of a pine stick 2.5 by 2.5 by 15 cm on a 4 by 4 cm foot, 80 g, standing in a tray (8 cm square inside) centered at (22, -14). Blue-tinted water stands 6 cm above the table in both with both in their trays. To build it: a 1 L clear jar with a bulkhead hose fitting in its bottom, clear vinyl tubing and an acrylic tube taped to a stick (reservoir-type water levels are sold the same way: a jug on a long clear hose with a clear end tube), two pine posts, a 2.5 cm board for the pad, a small rimmed shelf screwed to the far post, and a stiff red plastic clip with a tab and a pointer for the marker.
scoring: Doing nothing scores 0. The score is 0 for good if more than 1 mL (about 20 drops) runs out of a mouth, which happens when the end stands lower than the water (left in its tray, or put back while the jar is up) or the jar tips: in a real room that water lands on a wall or a finished floor. It is 0 too if the hose is pulled taut, since a taut hose drags the jar or the end over. A mark counts only if the marker's last move (more than 0.5 mm, the finest a steel rule reads) was a transfer: the jar within 3 cm of its spot 1 cm off the datum post, within 15 degrees of upright, gripped by its handle by the hand not on the marker, and the water surface inside it within 1.5 mm of the line (the jar itself straddles the line: its bottom is about 7 cm up and the line crosses its side about 6 cm up); the end's tube within 2.5 cm of its spot behind the pointer, within 15 degrees of upright; and the marker's edge within 1.5 mm of the end's water. A mark set from memory, or nudged after the jar comes down, copies nothing, and one hand cannot hold the jar on the line and slide a marker 45 cm away. The marker must be let go, because a clip still pinched can still move. Then 1.0 if the mark is within 1.5 mm (about 0.06 inch, finish tolerance for a ledger or cabinets) of the datum height and the jar and the end stand back in their trays (within 2.5 cm, bottom within 5 mm of the table, within 10 degrees of upright, under 1 cm/s, every tool point and pad tip 1 cm clear). Putting them back matters because lowering the jar before the end is the second place water spills, and a jar left held or propped can tip. 0.75 for the same mark with either not back: the mark, which is the job's product, is good, but the put-away is not done. 0.5 for a transfer and a mark only within 3 mm (about 0.12 inch): good enough for rough framing but not for a ledger, so it earns half. Otherwise 0.25 if the level was ever held set up for 1 s in a row (the end's tube at its spot, the jar gripped by its handle at its spot, both within 15 degrees of upright, the water level in the jar within 3 mm of the line). That credits the right order of moves and the jar held on the line, the hard first half, with no mark yet; the 1 s keeps a jar swept past the line from counting. Arm positions are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Success: 1.0 held 1 s. Real trial: measure the mark and the line from a laser line with a steel rule to 0.5 mm; weigh the level before and after (1 g = 1 mL); read tilts with a protractor on a video frame and hold times from the timestamps; and watch the video for the water level in the jar sitting at the line while the marker last moved, and for the hose pulled straight.
reset_notes: Stand the jar and the hose end in their trays, top the water up to 6 cm above the table with both side by side, coil the hose between the trays, dry the table, and slide the marker down to 9.2 cm. Run with -E object_jitter=0 (one fixed layout).
fidelity: The water is a model (levelhose), not particles. One surface height holds a fixed volume and is found every step from the jar's and the tube's poses. That is the hydrostatics a real level obeys, but it re-levels instantly (a real one takes about a second). A mouth below the water overflows at the Torricelli rate. The hose is drawn, not a body; taut means too short to span. A real trial measures the mark and weighs the spill instead. The jar is 150 g; a real one with its water is about 0.5 kg.
